Our editorial process produces two outputs: (i) public reviews designed to be posted alongside the preprint for the benefit of readers; (ii) feedback on the manuscript for the authors, including requests for revisions, shown below. We also include an acceptance summary that explains what the editors found interesting or important about the work.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Cortical Betz cells analogue in songbirds utilizes Kv3.1 to generate ultranarrow spikes" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 3 peer reviewers, one of whom is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors, and the evaluation has been overseen by John Huguenard as the Senior Editor. The following individual involved in the review of your submission has agreed to reveal their identity: Ian D Forsythe (Reviewer #1).

The reviewers have discussed their reviews with one another, and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this to help you prepare a revised submission.

Essential revisions:

1) The correspondence between RA cells and cortical Betz cells is a stretch.

This seems more of a discussion point than an essential part of the title, abstract, or introduction.

2) The evidence of a specific role for Kv3.1 is not conclusive and relevant claims should be moderated.

3) A valuable pharmacological approach is used. Evidence of stability of responses and reversibility of drug effects should be provided for each of the major findings.

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

This is an extensive piece of work and it contains some good quality data, but the great breadth of the article means that many elements of the results are too superficial and/or lack sufficient detail to deal with certain aspects and complexities of Kv3 physiology. There are also some problems in the interpretation of the voltage-clamp data which together weaken the overall findings.

1). Page 1. The first paragraph of the introduction over-emphasises a link to mammalian Betz cells; this would seem better justified as a discussion point. Perhaps you feel the need to justify the avian system to mammalian-biased readers, but the lack of transgenic zebrafinch models undermines the strength of your arguments for doing this work in the bird.

2) Page 3. Morphology. While the detail and work conducted in contrasting the morphology of RA and AId neurons are appreciated, your cell numbers are low (only 2 AId neurons) and this reduces the confidence in the observed differences. Also, many of the parameters are presented as % differences – this would be better presented as different absolute values (these are often only shown on the figure graph and are difficult to estimate). It is not clear how the observed differences relate to the Kv3 question, other than in establishing some convergence with mouse cortical neurons. This could be a distinct study in itself but is not a good fit for this manuscript.

3) Page 4 ln 179. Electrophysiology. The data is usefully presented in absolute terms in Table 1, but the differences should be described in the same terms, not as % (as in ln192) nor as qualitative comments (as in lns 198 – 203).

4) Page 5, ln 208-217. This is a methodological aside and is not relevant except to demonstrate the care that the authors have taken to exclude inhibitory neurons from their data set.

5) Page 5, ln 230-254. The data is consistent with a larger effect of TEA and 4-AP on RA repolarization. Again, absolute measures of duration rather than % change should be quoted and compared for the data in figure 4. This will be important if anyone were to model these conductances and neuronal properties in the future. APs in the Ald neurons are already longer, so a similar effect of TEA or 4AP might be expected to be proportionally smaller (if presented as %).

Figure 4 clearly shows that TEA and 4-AP have direct effects on the AP of RA cells, but less so on Aid cells. But you can only infer that this is mediated by an action on Kv3 channels. The data is very difficult to interpret as all the numerical graphs are presented in fold change in AP halfwidth. How long were the drugs applied, and was recovery data collected to demonstrate washout? It is a pedantic point, but have you checked that the pharmacological evidence cited (from mammals) applies to birds? Since you show no effect in Supl Figure 4, a key issue would be: does α-DTx or iberiotoxin block Kv1 and BK channels (respectively) in the bird; have you positive controls or can you provide citations of such (or at least checked for precise homology at the respective toxin binding sites)?

6) The effect of TEA and 4AP differs in figure 5 (first AP) from figure 4 (AP train). The effect on the half-width of the 1st AP seems smaller than on subsequent APs in the train – particularly noticeable in 5A and 5B. What is the explanation for this (see point 8 below)?

7) The AP duration is also changing during the trains in Supl Figure 5. There are a few minor inconsistencies here. For example, XE991 has a significant effect in the lowest current injections in S5c. The control peak firing rates (spikes/sec) in S5E are lower (~70 vs ~100) than in S5A and S5C.

8) Page 6 and figure 6. Voltage-clamp data is well presented and clearly shows larger outward currents in the RA neurons, with little or no 'low-voltage-activated' (steps to -30 mV; potential DTx-sensitive current) in either neuron type. The 'high-voltage activated' currents are very slow activating… And so would be hardly activated during a single fast AP lasting less than a ms….. This undermines your arguments that this is Kv3 on two counts: it is too slow to activate (taking over 100ms) and only differs by around 25% between RA and AId neurons. The key current for the AP repolarization, especially for the first AP in a train, is most likely to be the fast inactivating current. From the evidence in figure 6, it is not clear that this is a classic A-current (Kv4), because no estimation of steady-state inactivation has been conducted.

Although this undermines your current hypothesis that this is a Kv3.1 current, the possibility that the Kv3 current is fast inactivating (i.e. a Kv3.3 or Kv3.4-like current) is very interesting. In Figure 6G, you appear to show that both the inactivating and slow-activating outward currents are TEA-sensitive. Because the activation of the slow outward current overlaps with the decay of the fast transient outward current, any estimation of one will be contaminated by the other. Ideally, you could steady-state inactivate the transient current so you can measure the slow-activating current. This would then allow you to estimate the 'contamination' of one current by the other.

9) P7 ln 335. Another paper has described kcnc3/Kv3.3 in a seabird (De Paoli-Iseppi et al. PLOS One 12: e0189181, 2017).

10) Figure 7 and Page 7/8. The heading on ln 319 states, that Kv3.1 is the TEA-sensitive ion channel subunit… But this seems a rather weak point and could be disputed, as you have measured mRNA, not protein (and the interpretation of the current is ambiguous). The in situ hybridisation for each of the Kv3 genes is interesting, but the quantification is insufficient. The lack of absolute values (or at least relative to some 'housekeeping' gene) for the mRNA expression is a serious weakness. The ratios expressed here between two nuclei in Figure 7 hide/obscure important information and have contributed to the misinterpretation of the physiology. For example, one could argue on the basis of Fig7A that all Kv3 genes are present and that kcnc3 is most striking in that it highlights the two nuclei of interest, is present in both and you have the positive control of Purkinje neurons. Fig7B and 7C are best omitted… The expression ratio of RA to Ald has little or no relevance to a measurable parameter in your study. Perhaps you could argue some relevance if you had done a more quantitative measure and/or western blotting, but this has not been done. Your own evidence clearly indicates that multiple Kv3 subunits are present (Figure 7A), but you have no measure of the efficacy with which the mRNA is translated into protein (it is also hard to know what constitutes a 'background' value for any of the mRNA probes).

11. AUT5. This is not a well-designed experiment, since you apply a dose that is half-maximal (1uM when the EC50 is 1.3uM: ln 391), so you would be unlikely to observe more than half of the potential effect. For most readers, this comes across as a rather minor point and I think they will wonder why they need to know this information, certainly it is a weak figure with which to finish. Perhaps if AUT5 was shown to change the finch song or other behaviour in the opposite way to blocking the channel it would be interesting. AUT5 effects have also been noted previously in other publications:

Eur J Pharmacol. 2758:164-70.

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

This paper was a pleasure to read and goes through a logical sequence of experiments to pinpoint the role of Kv3(.1?) in the fast-spiking of RAPN neurons. There are large replicate numbers for almost all findings, and admirably, there is confirmation of the main result at physiological temperature. The phase plots in Figure 4 make clear that 4AP and TEA, at the concentrations used, have little effect on Ald neurons, but strong effects on RAPNs in both current clamp and voltage clamp. The methods developed to improve voltage clamp compliance are to be commended.

1) The paper has an unclear focus. In some ways, it focuses on the properties of RAPN neurons and how they might generate fast APs. Yet in other contexts, the paper seems to center on the description of a previously uncharacterized cell type, the neurons of Ald.

2) The pharmacological analysis of repetitive spike firing is lacking. For example, the traces in Figure 5B and 5D, and 8B and 8D, DO in fact show effects of 4AP/TEA/AUT5 on Ald neurons. This raised two issues. A) Repeated measures, such as a paired t-test I (before and after the drug, on a per cell basis) are arguably more appropriate than group averages at each current injection strength. B) Some effort should be dedicated to reversibility. While it can be technically challenging to hold a cell for the total time required to completely wash out the drug, at least a few examples should be provided to confirm that "drug" effects are not due to time-dependent changes in cell physiology.

3) For fast repolarization, it would likely be better to focus mainly on the early current, highlight with the red bars in figure 6, rather than on the current persisting until 200 ms.

4) There is a bit of circular logic regarding the description of the effects of AUT5 on spike depolarization (Figure 8A). If RA affects the maximum depolarization, then this could secondarily increase the recruitment of K channels and in turn produce a faster rate of repolarization.

5) While voltage clamp compliance is likely much improved by the approaches taken, it will still not be perfect, and there will remain issues of non-isopotentiality. This should be discussed.

6) The correspondence to Betz cells is oversold and should be removed from the title and abstract. There are many differences, as the authors note. A) The RA cells are not necessarily larger than other motor output neurons as with Betz cells, B) They have presumably developed along a unique evolutionary path, C) Other central features of Betz cells (conduction velocities, myelination, axon fiber diameter) are not reported.

claims.claim: In response to 100 µM 4-AP, RAPNs showed a 35% decrease in maximum repolarization rate compared to 8% in AId neurons.

claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding of the current study, supported by data in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Upon exposure to TEA, RAPNs showed significant decreases in the evoked firing rate (35 ± 4.1% decrease in spikes/s, 29.3 ± 10.4% decrease in instantaneous firing, and 33.7 ± 3.8% decrease in steady-state firing frequency upon the +500 pA current injection).
claims.source: Upon exposure to TEA, RAPNs showed significant decreases in the evoked firing rate (Figure 5A; 35 ± 4.1% decrease in spikes/s, 29.3 ± 10.4% decrease in instantaneous firing, and 33.7 ± 3.8% decrease in steady-state firing frequency upon the +500 pA current injection), whereas trends, but no significant effects, were seen in AId (Figure 5B).

claims.claim: Upon exposure to 4-AP, RAPNs showed significant decreases in the evoked firing rate (36.8 ± 10.9% decrease in spikes/s, 63.7 ± 4.8% decrease in instantaneous firing frequency, and 36.5 ± 12.9% decrease in steady-state firing frequency upon the +500 pA current injection).
claims.source: Upon exposure to 4-AP, RAPNs also showed significant decreases in the evoked firing rate (Figure 5C; 36.8 ± 10.9% decrease in spikes/s, 63.7 ± 4.8% decrease in instantaneous firing frequency, and 36.5 ± 12.9% decrease in steady-state firing frequency upon the +500 pA current injection), whereas trends, but no significant effects, were seen in AId (Figure 5D).

claims.claim: Kv3.x subunits are the predominant TEA- and 4-AP-sensitive channels in the recorded arcopallial cells.

claims.claim: RAPNs produced significantly larger peak outward currents 200 ms after stepping to 0 mV (12.2±1.2 nA) compared to AId neurons (4.8±0.7 nA).

claims.claim: The time to peak of the A-type current component was shorter in RAPNs (4.7±0.4 ms) than in AId neurons (6.2±0.3 ms).

claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding of the current study, supported by voltage-clamp data in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Upon washing in 500 µM TEA, RAPNs showed a larger fold change in both the peak of the A-type current component (55.7±4.4% decrease) and in the peak current at I200ms (41.2±5.2% decrease) compared to AId neurons (22.0 ± 4.9% and 22.2 ± 7.0% decrease, respectively).

claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding of the current study, supported by voltage-clamp data in Figure 6.

claims.claim: RAPNs had a significantly larger TEA-sensitive IK+ than AId neurons, whether measuring the A-type current peak (4.7±0.4 nA vs. 1.1±0.3 nA) or the I200ms peak (5.0±0.7 nA vs. 1.3±0.5 nA).
claims.source: Importantly, whether measuring the A-type current peak (Figure 6I; mean ± SE: 4.7±0.4 nA vs. 1.1±0.3 nA for RAPNs and AId neurons, respectively) or the I200ms peak (Figure 6J; mean ± SE: 5.0±0.7 nA vs. 1.3±0.5 nA for RAPNs and AId neurons, respectively), RAPNs had a significantly larger TEA-sensitive IK+ than AId neurons.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding of the current study, supported by voltage-clamp data in Figure 6.

claims.claim: The locus named KCNC1 (100144433; located on chromosome 5) is the zebra finch ortholog of mammalian KCNC1.
claims.source: As a start, through close assessments of reciprocal alignments and synteny we confirmed that the locus named KCNC1 (100144433; located on chromosome 5) is the zebra finch ortholog of mammalian KCNC1, noting the conserved synteny across major vertebrate groups (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding of the current study based on comparative genomic analysis.

claims.claim: The predicted zebra finch Kv3.1 protein (Kv3.1b isoform) is remarkably conserved (96.5% residue identity) with human.
claims.source: Importantly, the predicted zebra finch Kv3.1 protein (Kv3.1b isoform) is remarkably conserved (96.5% residue identity) with human (Figure 7—figure supplement 2) and is thus predicted to have similar pharmacology as in mammals, which is supported by our recordings from RAPNs.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding of the current study based on sequence analysis.

claims.claim: LOC115491734 is the zebra finch ortholog of mammalian KCNC3, previously thought to be missing in birds.
claims.source: We conclude that LOC115491734 is the zebra finch ortholog of mammalian KCNC3, previously thought to be missing in birds (Lovell et al., 2013), and not KCNC1.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding of the current study based on comparative genomic analysis.

claims.claim: The predicted zebra finch KCNC3 protein showed only moderate conservation with human (68.32% residue identity).
claims.source: The predicted zebra finch KCNC3 protein showed only moderate conservation with human (68.32% residue identity), some domains including the BTB/POZ and transmembrane domain being fairly conserved, but spans of residues on the N-terminal and C-terminal regions being highly divergent.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding of the current study based on sequence analysis.

claims.claim: Based on the genomic sequence, the N-terminal inactivation domain is absent in the predicted zebra finch KCNC3 protein.
claims.source: Notably, based on the genomic sequence, the N-terminal inactivation domain (Rudy and McBain, 2001) is absent in the predicted zebra finch KCNC3 protein (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding of the current study based on sequence analysis.

claims.claim: KCNC1/Kv3.1 expression is higher in RA than in AId.
claims.source: We replicated our previous finding that KCNC1/Kv3.1 expression is higher in RA than in AId (Nevue et al., 2020; Figure 7A, top left), whereas expression of both Kv3.2 (Figure 7A, top right) and Kv3.4 (Figure 7A, bottom right) was non-differential between RA and AId.

claims.claim: Expression of Kv3.2 and Kv3.4 was non-differential between RA and AId.

claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding of the current study, supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Kv3.1 expression was uniformly distributed across RA.
claims.source: Unlike the graded Kv3.1 expression that matches a tonotopic distribution found in avian (Parameshwaran et al., 2001) and mammalian (Li et al., 2001) auditory brainstem, Kv3.1 expression was uniformly distributed across RA.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding of the current study, contrasting with expression patterns in other brain regions.

claims.claim: Kv3.2-expressing cells were sparse, strongly labeled, and reminiscent of the GABAergic cell distribution.
claims.source: Kv3.2-expressing cells were sparse, strongly labeled, and reminiscent of the GABAergic cell distribution (Pinaud and Mello, 2007), while Kv3.4 expression was uniformly weak throughout both brain regions (Figure 7A).

claims.claim: Kv3.4 expression was uniformly weak throughout both RA and AId.
claims.source: Kv3.2-expressing cells were sparse, strongly labeled, and reminiscent of the GABAergic cell distribution (Pinaud and Mello, 2007), while Kv3.4 expression was uniformly weak throughout both brain regions (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding of the current study, supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Kv3.3, while more strongly expressed in both RA and AId compared to the surrounding arcopallium, is non-differentially expressed between RA and AId.
claims.source: We also found that Kv3.3, while more strongly expressed in both brain regions compared to the surrounding arcopallium, is non-differentially expressed between RA and AId (Figure 7A, bottom left).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding of the current study, supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Strong Kv3.3 expression was found in the Purkinje cell layer of the cerebellum.
claims.source: Importantly, we found strong Kv3.3 expression in the Purkinje cell layer of the cerebellum (Figure 7A, bottom left), consistent with findings in mammals (Akemann and Knöpfel, 2006).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding of the current study, supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 7.

claims.claim: KCNQ2 had a lower proportion of labeled cells in RA than in AId.
claims.source: Furthermore, other TEA-sensitive potassium channel subunits examined, namely members of the Kv1 (KCNA), BK (KCNMA), and Kv7 (KCNQ) families, had similar expression in RA and AId, with the exception of KCNQ2, which had a lower proportion of labeled cells in RA than in AId (Figure 7B and C).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding of the current study, supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 7.

claims.claim: KCNC1/Kv3.1 is the only TEA-sensitive subunit examined that was more highly expressed in RA compared to AId.
claims.source: These results indicate that compared to the other TEA-sensitive channels, KCNC1/Kv3.1 is the only TEA-sensitive subunit we examined that was more highly expressed in RA compared to AId, providing supporting evidence for a stronger contribution of Kv3.1 in shaping the ultranarrow AP of RAPNs compared to AId neurons.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the in situ hybridization data.

claims.claim: The morphology of RAPNs described in this study is consistent with previous morphological characterizations.

claims.claim: The higher dendritic branch complexity and higher number of dendritic spines of AId neurons suggest that AId may receive more synaptic inputs than RAPNs.
claims.source: The higher dendritic branch complexity revealed by a Sholl analysis (Sholl, 1956b) and the higher number of dendritic spines (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) of AId neurons (a finding revealed using two methods: FIJI, Schindelin et al., 2012, and ShuTu, Jin et al., 2019) suggest that AId may receive more synaptic inputs than RAPNs.

claims.claim: The higher proportion of large spines in RAPNs than in AId neurons parallels Betz cells, which also contain higher proportions of large spines compared to other pyramidal neurons within the cat M1.

claims.claim: The differences in spine shape and surface area between RAPNs and AId neurons suggest potential differences in filtering of incoming synaptic signals.

claims.claim: The spine density difference between RAPNs and AId neurons closely approximates findings in the high vocal center (HVC), where upstream HVC-RA projecting neurons exhibit roughly half the spine density as HVC-Area X projecting neurons.
claims.source: Of note, the spine density difference between RAPNs and AId neurons closely approximates findings in the high vocal center (HVC), where upstream HVC-RA projecting neurons exhibit roughly half the spine density as HVC-Area X projecting neurons (Kornfeld et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a comparison with findings in another brain region, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Based on their larger overall spine surface area, AId neurons are investing more 'resources' on spines than RAPNs, despite having proportionately smaller individual spines.
claims.source: Based on their larger overall spine surface area, it appears that AId neurons are investing more 'resources' on spines than RAPNs, despite having proportionately smaller individual spines.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the morphological data.

claims.claim: The sparse population of large spines in adult male RAPNs may indicate larger synaptic inputs per spine compared to AId neurons.

claims.claim: Large, stable and mature spines in RAPNs may enable large EPSCs in adult RAPNs from male birds with crystallized songs.
claims.source: Large, stable and mature spines in RAPNs may thus enable large EPSCs in adult RAPNs from male birds with crystallized songs (Garst-Orozco et al., 2014; Kittelberger and Mooney, 1999).

claims.claim: The speed and accuracy of fine muscle control in mammals requires the firing of L5PNs that project from the primary motor cortex (M1) to various targets in the brainstem and spinal cord.
claims.source: The speed and accuracy of fine muscle control in mammals requires the firing of L5PNs that project from the primary motor cortex (M1) to various targets in the brainstem and spinal cord (Oswald et al., 2013; Suter et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about mammalian motor control, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Upper motor RAPNs and L5PNs in mammalian M1 share factors determining AP initiation and upstroke, including APs with biphasic depolarization rates, persistent Na+ currents, large transient Na+ currents (INaT) with rapid kinetics, and high Navβ4 mRNA expression.
claims.source: We have recently described how upper motor RAPNs and L5PNs in mammalian M1 also share factors determining AP initiation and upstroke. This includes APs with biphasic depolarization rates, persistent Na+ currents, large transient Na+ currents (INaT) with rapid kinetics, and high Navβ4 mRNA expression, which we showed to be linked to robust resurgent currents (INaR) in RAPNs (Zemel et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from a previous study by the authors, supported by citation.

claims.claim: High Navβ4 mRNA expression is linked to robust resurgent currents (INaR) in RAPNs.
claims.source: We have recently described how upper motor RAPNs and L5PNs in mammalian M1 also share factors determining AP initiation and upstroke. This includes APs with biphasic depolarization rates, persistent Na+ currents, large transient Na+ currents (INaT) with rapid kinetics, and high Navβ4 mRNA expression, which we showed to be linked to robust resurgent currents (INaR) in RAPNs (Zemel et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from a previous study by the authors, supported by citation.

claims.claim: The 1.2 ms AP half-width at 24°C and the 'regular' minimally adapting AP firing of AId neurons render them more similar to canonical L5PNs in the motor cortex of rodents, cats, and primates.
claims.source: In contrast to RAPNs, the 1.2 ms AP half-width at 24°C and the 'regular' minimally adapting AP firing of AId neurons render them more similar to canonical L5PNs in the motor cortex of rodents (Lacey et al., 2014), cats (Chen et al., 1996), and primates (Vigneswaran et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a comparison with mammalian L5PNs, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Previous comparative studies in the auditory system have suggested convergent strategies for temporal coding of sound stimuli in birds and mammals.

claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous studies, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Like Betz cells, RAPNs appear to be a specialized class of upper motor neurons that display higher temporal precision of AP firing and faster firing rates than AId neurons.
claims.source: Our data suggest similar convergence in the motor control circuitry where, like Betz cells (Bakken et al., 2021; Ichinohe et al., 2004; Soares et al., 2017), RAPNs appear to be a specialized class of upper motor neurons that display higher temporal precision of AP firing and faster firing rates than AId neurons.

claims.claim: RAPNs and AId neurons lack the large, tufted apical dendrites typical of L5PNs.

claims.claim: RAPNs and AId neurons fire spontaneously in the absence of synaptic inputs, a property not typically seen in M1 L5PNs.
claims.source: Additionally, these avian neurons fire spontaneously in the absence of synaptic inputs, a property not typically seen in M1 L5PNs (Chen et al., 1996; Lacey et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a difference between finch neurons and mammalian L5PNs, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Betz cells have very large somas and are interspersed with smaller L5PNs.
claims.source: Whereas Betz cells have very large somas and are interspersed with smaller L5PNs (Lassek, 1940; Rivara et al., 2003), RAPNs and AId neurons have similar soma sizes and localize to adjacent but distinct regions within the finch arcopallium (Bottjer et al., 2000; Johnson et al., 1995; Nevue et al., 2020).

claims.claim: RAPNs and AId neurons have similar soma sizes and localize to adjacent but distinct regions within the finch arcopallium.

claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding of the current study and previous studies, supported by citations.

claims.claim: By quickly activating at depolarized voltages, Kv3 channels can efficiently initiate Nav channel recovery from inactivation during repetitive AP firing.
claims.source: By quickly activating at depolarized voltages, Kv3 channels can efficiently initiate Nav channel recovery from inactivation during repetitive AP firing (Bean, 2007; Gu et al., 2018; Kaczmarek and Zhang, 2017; Rudy and McBain, 2001).

claims.claim: The narrowing of the AP waveform and increase in steady-state firing by AUT5 provide support for a stronger contribution of Kv3.1 in the repolarization of APs and in increasing the availability of Nav channels during high-frequency firing in RAPNs versus AId neurons.

claims.claim: The fact that the AUT5 effects on Kv3.1-expressing zebra finch neurons were similar to those seen in mammals is not surprising, as the predicted peptide sequence of finch Kv3.1 is ~96.5% identical to that of the human Kv3.1b splice variant.

claims.claim: Birds and mammals diverged 300 million years ago.

claims.claim: The remarkable conservation of Kv3.1 suggests that Kv3.1 channels may be optimized for enabling ultranarrow AP waveforms and high-frequency firing.

results.result: RAPNs and AId neurons exhibit distinct morphological features. AId neurons show higher dendritic complexity, higher spine density, and smaller spines compared to RAPNs, which have larger mushroom-type spines similar to Betz cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C60 are supported by morphological data in Figure 1, including Sholl analysis (C56), spine counts (C58), and spine shape characterization (C59-C60). The data consistently show morphological differences between RAPNs and AId neurons with appropriate statistical analysis (p-values reported).

results.result: RAPNs exhibit ultranarrow action potentials with significantly faster repolarization rates compared to AId neurons. At room temperature, RAPNs show AP half-widths approximately half that of AId neurons (0.53 vs 1.24 ms), with 76% larger maximum repolarization rates.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C37, C62-C67 are strongly supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 2 and Table 1. The measurements show consistent differences in AP half-width and repolarization rates at both room temperature and 40°C, with appropriate statistical tests (p-values < 0.001).

results.result: RAPNs fire at significantly higher frequencies than AId neurons during both spontaneous activity and evoked responses. The slower repolarization rate of AId neurons likely limits their capacity for high-frequency repetitive spiking.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C38, C68-C70 are supported by data in Figure 3 showing firing rate differences at multiple current injection levels. The inference about repolarization rate limiting firing frequency (C70) is reasonable given the strong correlation between repolarization rate and firing frequency differences.

results.result: Kv3 channel blockers (TEA and 4-AP) disproportionately affect RAPNs compared to AId neurons, causing greater AP broadening (77% vs 36% for TEA) and larger decreases in firing rates in RAPNs, indicating differential Kv3 channel activity between the two cell types.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C41, C78-C83 are supported by pharmacological data in Figures 4-5. The differential effects of TEA and 4-AP on AP waveform and firing rates are consistently demonstrated with appropriate statistical analysis. The conclusion about differential Kv3 activity is well-supported by the data.

results.result: Other K+ channel blockers (α-dendrotoxin, XE991, iberiotoxin) targeting Kv1, Kv7, and BK channels showed no significant effects on AP properties in either RAPNs or AId neurons, indicating that Kv3.x subunits are the predominant TEA- and 4-AP-sensitive channels in these cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C85 are supported by negative control experiments in Figure 4—figure supplement 2. The lack of effects from selective blockers of other K+ channels strengthens the conclusion that Kv3.x channels are responsible for the observed TEA/4-AP sensitivity.

results.result: Voltage-clamp recordings reveal that RAPNs produce significantly larger TEA-sensitive outward K+ currents than AId neurons (12.2 vs 4.8 nA at 0 mV), with faster activation kinetics. TEA application caused larger proportional reductions in both A-type and sustained K+ currents in RAPNs compared to AId neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C89 are supported by voltage-clamp data in Figure 6. The measurements show clear differences in current amplitudes and TEA sensitivity between RAPNs and AId neurons with appropriate statistical analysis. The data provide direct evidence for differential Kv3 channel expression.

results.result: In situ hybridization reveals that KCNC1 (Kv3.1) is the only Kv3 family member with significantly higher expression in RA compared to AId, while KCNC2-4 (Kv3.2-3.4) show non-differential expression. Among all TEA-sensitive K+ channel subunits examined, only KCNC1 shows preferential expression in RA.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C45, C95-C103 are supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 7. The differential expression of KCNC1 is clearly demonstrated, while other Kv3 family members and TEA-sensitive channels show similar expression patterns. This provides strong molecular evidence linking Kv3.1 to the unique properties of RAPNs.

results.result: Comparative genomic analysis identified zebra finch KCNC3 (Kv3.3), a gene previously thought to be absent in birds. The zebra finch Kv3.1 protein shows remarkable conservation with human (96.5% identity), while Kv3.3 shows moderate conservation (68.32%) and lacks the N-terminal inactivation domain present in mammalian Kv3.3.
results.evaluation: Claims C46, C90-C94 are supported by comparative genomic analysis and sequence alignments shown in Figure 7 supplements. The identification of KCNC3 in zebra finch is a novel finding supported by synteny analysis and sequence comparisons. The high conservation of Kv3.1 is well-documented.

results.result: The Kv3.1/3.2 positive modulator AUT5 selectively narrows AP waveforms (6.5% decrease), increases maximum repolarization rates (12.2% increase), and enhances steady-state firing frequency (24.3% increase) in RAPNs but not in AId neurons, providing functional evidence for differential Kv3.1 contribution.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C43, C104-C107, C127 are supported by pharmacological data in Figure 8. The selective effects of AUT5 on RAPNs provide strong functional evidence for differential Kv3.1 expression and activity. The lack of effect in AId neurons serves as an important control.

results.result: RAPNs share molecular and electrophysiological properties with primate Betz cells, including ultranarrow spikes, high Kv3.1 expression, and large spines. This suggests convergent evolution of Kv3.1-dependent mechanisms for precise, rapid firing in upper motor neurons controlling fast and complex motor skills in songbirds and primates.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7, C10, C51-C52, C121, C159 represent the main conclusion of the study. The convergent evolution hypothesis is well-supported by the comprehensive data showing similarities between RAPNs and Betz cells in spike properties, Kv3.1 expression, and morphology, combined with the known absence of Betz cells in rodents and the specialized motor functions in both systems.

results.result: The morphological differences between RAPNs and AId neurons suggest functional implications: AId neurons may receive more synaptic inputs due to higher spine density, while RAPNs' larger spines may indicate larger synaptic inputs per spine, potentially contributing to stereotyped song production.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C115 are largely speculative inferences from morphological data. While the morphological differences are well-documented (supported), the functional implications regarding synaptic input strength and song stereotypy (C114-C115) are speculations that require direct electrophysiological measurements of synaptic currents and correlation with behavioral data.

results.result: The molecular and electrophysiological similarities between RAPNs and AId neurons suggest these regions may share a common evolutionary origin, with RA potentially evolving as a specialized expansion of AId for vocal motor control.
results.evaluation: Claims C157-C158 propose an evolutionary relationship based on shared properties. While the similarities are well-documented, the evolutionary inference requires additional comparative data across species and developmental studies. The hypothesis is plausible but not definitively proven by the current data.

results.result: Background knowledge claims establish the functional roles of RAPNs and AId neurons, properties of Betz cells, and the known expression of Kv3.1 in these cell types, providing context for the current study.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C16-C36 are background knowledge claims supported by appropriate citations. These establish the context and motivation for the study, including the known properties of RAPNs, Betz cells, and Kv3 channels from previous literature.

results.result: Previous work established that RAPNs share Nav channel properties with mammalian L5PNs, including high Navβ4 expression linked to resurgent currents. The combination of Navβ4 and Kv3 channels likely promotes ultranarrow spikes and rapid bursting, with developmental and regional differences in expression correlating with firing properties.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C118, C148-C152 summarize previous findings from the authors and others, appropriately cited. These provide important context for understanding how Kv3.1 works in concert with Nav channels to produce the unique properties of RAPNs.

results.result: RAPNs and AId neurons share several electrophysiological parameters and molecular markers (Nav1.1, Nav1.6, Navβ4, Kv3.3), distinguishing them from other arcopallial neurons that exhibit broader APs and lower expression of these channels.
results.evaluation: Claims C153-C156 are supported by data in Table 1 and previous studies (C154, C156). The shared properties help define RAPNs and AId as a related class of upper motor neurons distinct from other arcopallial populations.

results.result: The morphology of RAPNs described in this study is consistent with previous morphological characterizations, suggesting these neurons represent a fairly homogeneous cell type.
results.evaluation: Claim C108 is supported by comparison with previous studies (Kittelberger and Mooney, 1999; Spiro et al., 1999). The consistency with prior work validates the current morphological findings.

results.result: AId neurons resemble canonical mammalian L5PNs more than RAPNs do, based on AP half-width and firing patterns. However, both RAPNs and AId neurons differ from mammalian L5PNs in lacking tufted apical dendrites and exhibiting spontaneous firing. Comparative analysis suggests convergent evolution in motor control circuitry.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C125 are supported by comparisons with literature data on mammalian L5PNs and Betz cells. The similarities and differences are appropriately characterized, supporting the convergent evolution hypothesis while acknowledging important structural differences.

results.result: Background on Kv3 channel function, pharmacology, evolution, and disease relevance, including the role of Kv3.1 in various cell types, splice variants, and the interaction between Kv3 channels and Nav channels in promoting efficient, high-frequency firing.
results.evaluation: Claims C126, C128-C147 provide important background knowledge about Kv3 channels, appropriately cited. These establish the functional significance of Kv3.1 expression and provide context for interpreting the experimental findings.

results.result: This study identifies RAPNs as a novel and more accessible model for studying Betz-like pyramidal neurons that offer temporal precision required for complex learned motor behaviors.
results.evaluation: Claim C160 is a reasonable conclusion based on the comprehensive demonstration of similarities between RAPNs and Betz cells. The accessibility advantage of the zebra finch model is valid, though the claim about being 'more accessible' could benefit from explicit comparison of experimental challenges.
